statement: Student answer, praised by the teacher as the pain point: because of the hash in the where clause the database must read every row, compute each email's hash and compare it, a whole-table scan, before it can do the join.

statement: A classic way to build almost any system: you either query the source of truth, or you keep things pre-computed.
detail: The teacher addressed everyone: you would see this in almost every single system you implement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You either can query the source of truth, or you can keep things pre-computed.

statement: Query the source of truth directly when you need strong consistency; to get more efficiency, pre-compute the data or store it in a form that is directly consumable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Either you directly fire source of truth when you need strong consistency, or you may build, or to get more efficiency, you may pre-compute...

statement: With the pre-computed set you directly get its length as the number of unique senders, while the source-of-truth approach fires an expensive query - whether implemented in SQL or NoSQL does not matter.
case_study: Newly unread indicator: set length vs count(unique(from)) query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here you had to fire an expensive query, SQL, NoSQL implementation, anything, that does not matter.

statement: The cost of pre-computing: keeping the pre-computed data updated becomes our responsibility and needs another flow that also writes the data there, whereas the source of truth is updated by nature because all messages are ingested into it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now it's our responsibility to keep this updated. Here it was by nature, it was updated because it is actually the source of truth.

statement: Neither approach is wrong; it depends on what you prioritise and your scale: for a startup querying the source of truth works just fine, but as millions of people become concurrently active you may be tempted to go with the pre-computed approach.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As a startup, this would work just fine for you folks.

statement: The Redis cluster is overburdened: it serves a huge number of reads (millions of users refreshing or moving between pages call the get API), plus a large number of writes when users click the message icon, plus an update on every message-unsent event.

statement: The database is the most brittle component of an infrastructure, so check whether you are doing unnecessary operations on it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as I always say, database is the most brittle component of an infrastructure.

statement: The get status path is already the bare minimum: you must go to the database because it is the source of truth, and a read replica is not needed because it is an in-memory DB anyway.

statement: For the N-1 repeat messages the write still calls the database although the set already holds the sender, wasting network I/O and, more importantly, making the database handle those requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no changes happening in the DB, but you would still make a call to DB trying to write to the set.

statement: For each such write the database receives the request, reads the set, checks whether the entry exists, and discards it if it does (adds it if not) - a lot of work that changes nothing for the N-1 cases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It would get the request. It would read the set, see if the entry exists in the set. It would discard.

statement: High-level pattern: whenever a database is doing a lot of unnecessary operations that lead to no state change, minimise them, because the database is the most brittle component - no matter which cloud provider you pick, if the database is down everything is down; protect it however you can.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you find a database that is doing a lot of unnecessary operations leading to no state changes in database, try to minimize them

statement: Use an auxiliary database to minimise the unnecessary operations on the primary database: when a brittle component (typically the database) does many operations that change nothing, add an auxiliary database and reduce the load on the main one so the service stays up.

statement: Adding the auxiliary database costs one more network I/O, but preventing the main database from going down by adding a bit of network cost is a good trade-off - worth it every single time.

statement: Auxiliary Redis write flow: the write first goes to the auxiliary Redis, which checks whether the entry (an unread message already exists from this sender) exists; if it exists, no write is made to the main database; if not, the write goes to the main database.

board_notes.statement: An auxiliary Redis sits in front of the main Redis cluster on the write path: workers record sender-recipient pairs (e.g. B_C : True, B_D : True) there and write to the main cluster only for a new pair; clearing status also deletes from the auxiliary store.

statement: With the auxiliary Redis the main database is not even called for the n-1 repeat messages; the auxiliary takes the bulk of those queries and all the hitting, while the main database is protected.

statement: Failure analysis: if the main database goes down everything is down anyway; if the auxiliary Redis goes down, all writes simply go to the main database, which handles the n-1 writes it was handling anyway - the auxiliary only sheds load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So by adding this auxiliary database, you are just trying to shed the load that was there on this main database.
